original_question: Can one develop a rigorous theory of soliton scattering for the nonlinear Schrodinger equation on graphs with nontrivial topology, especially trees, beyond the already treated star-graph and similar simple cases? In particular, how do network topology and the availability of Strichartz estimates affect the propagation and scattering of solitons on such graphs?
target_in_paper: §2.4, unnumbered open problem stated immediately after Lemma 2.4: extending the rigorous fast-soliton scattering analysis from the three-edge star graph/Y-junction to graphs with less trivial topology, especially trees, with Strichartz estimates identified as a necessary ingredient.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s actual open direction: going beyond the rigorously treated star-graph/Y-junction case to graphs with more complicated topology; it also correctly singles out trees, and it correctly emphasizes that dispersive/Strichartz estimates are a central technical obstacle for any such extension.
missing_details: The paper is not asking about arbitrary soliton scattering, but specifically about extending the fast-soliton scattering theory developed in §2.4.
The nearby rigorous model is the focusing cubic NLS, not a general-power NLS; the paper explicitly says the cubic assumption is essential for the treated result.

The benchmark case is a three-edge star graph (a Y-junction), presented with Kirchhoff vertex conditions in the exposition, though the author notes some other one-vertex selfadjoint conditions can also be treated.
The incoming state is a solitary wave initially placed far out on one edge and moving with large velocity toward the vertex; the relevant asymptotic regime is the high-velocity regime.

What is proved in the star-graph case is a post-collision approximation by reflected and transmitted outgoing waves, with masses/amplitudes linked to the linear scattering coefficients of the underlying linear graph Hamiltonian.
The paper stresses that the rigorous control in the treated star-graph result is in L^2-type mass transmission/reflection estimates, not a full outgoing-profile theorem in a stronger norm.
The paper’s open problem concerns metric graphs with less trivial topology, especially trees; it is not framed as a general question about all possible networks or arbitrary graph topologies.

The nearby context also notes that, at the time of writing, even well-posedness of NLS on trees had not yet been proved, although dispersive estimates on suitable trees/networks were available; this is part of why the question is delicate.
The paper distinguishes this topology problem from easier extensions on star graphs, such as more than three edges, some bound-state cases, and certain other selfadjoint boundary conditions.
refined_question: For the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation i∂tΨ = HΨ - |Ψ|^2Ψ on a metric graph whose topology is more complicated than a star graph—most notably on a tree, with H the selfadjoint graph Schrödinger/Laplacian operator determined by the vertex conditions—can one prove a fast-soliton scattering theorem analogous to the three-edge Y-junction result of §2.4? More precisely, starting from an incoming high-velocity solitary wave placed on one external edge, can one show that after interaction with the branching vertices the solution is, on the corresponding post-collision timescale, approximated in the same L^2/mass-transfer sense by reflected/transmitted outgoing waves whose weights are governed by the linear scattering data of H, under hypotheses that ensure the linear dispersive/Strichartz estimates required by the star-graph analysis?
justification: The draft is targeting the unnumbered open problem in §2.4, not the standing-wave material. The author first recalls the only rigorous scattering result discussed in the paper: fast-soliton scattering for the cubic NLS on a three-edge star graph/Y-junction, where outgoing reflected/transmitted waves are described through the linear scattering coefficients over a controlled post-collision timescale. He then explicitly says that scattering on graphs with less trivial topology is open, points in particular to trees, and adds that Strichartz estimates are among the main technical ingredients and are needed for any generalization. The rewrite therefore keeps the question tightly anchored to that exact extension problem, rather than broadening it to a general theory of arbitrary soliton dynamics on arbitrary graphs.
